Henry Eni-Otu, a Nigerian constitutional lawyer, has identified loopholes in the Electoral Act provisions that set limits on campaign donations, arguing the gaps could allow politicians and their supporters to circumvent the statutory threshold.
Section 92(8) of the Electoral Act prescribes that an individual or corporate organisation must not donate more than ₦500 million to any candidate contesting an election.
This means that no individual or corporate entity is permitted to donate more than ₦500 million to a single candidate, irrespective of the political office being contested.
However, as the 2027 general election approaches, several political allies of candidates, particularly presidential aspirants, have increasingly demonstrated their support through donations. While some are believed to be making cash contributions privately, others have donated brand-new vehicles, relief materials and other items to support campaign logistics.
One such instance is the donation of brand-new vehicles to states by Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, to support the re-election campaign of President Bola Tinubu.
Daily Trust recently estimated that Mr Ekpemupolo, a former militant leader and Grand Patron of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, donated more than 600 vehicles, valued at approximately ₦3.68 billion, to support Mr Tinubu’s re-election campaign across the states.
The PBAT Door-to-Door Movement is a political group mobilising support for Mr Tinubu’s re-election.

The donation has generated criticism from some Nigerians, particularly over concerns that it violates the Electoral Act’s provision limiting campaign donations by individuals and corporate organisations to ₦500 million.
However, Mr Eni-Otu examined the issue on Thursday during the inauguration of the 2027 General Elections Law Situation Room in Abuja.
The situation room is an initiative of Law Corridor, an Abuja-based law firm, established to examine pre- and post-election issues and promote voter education ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Mr Eni-Otu, the managing partner of Law Corridor, argued that although the Electoral Act prescribes a ₦500 million donation limit for individuals, the relevant provisions do not expressly extend the restriction to in-kind donations, such as vehicles, food items, and other commodities.
“By virtue of Section 92(2–9) of the Electoral Act, it is quite clear that the maximum donation by an individual to any candidate for an election, particularly for the office of the president, is ₦500 million.
“However, one very obvious lacuna which could be exploited by any individual is the fact that those provisions did not recognise that ₦500 million could be given in cash or in kind. So, that particular lacuna remains. The law only recognises cash donations; it does not recognise the equivalent of cash in kind,” he argued.
The lawyer maintained that, under the current provisions of the law, Mr Ekpemupolo’s donations have not breached the Electoral Act, despite the estimated value of the vehicles exceeding the statutory donation threshold.
He based his argument on the fact that the donations were made in the form of campaign vehicles, which, according to him, are not expressly covered by the donation restrictions in the Act.
“For today, considering the position of the law as it is now, the donation made by Tompolo in kind cannot be quantified, and even if quantified, by provisions of the law, the law has not in any manner outlawed the limit to which donations in kind can be given,” he said.
Mr Eni-Otu also addressed the High Court’s decision to disqualify Ovie Omo-Agege as the candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) for Delta Central Senatorial District and rule that the party would not be allowed to field a candidate for the election.
He argued that the court was right in its decision, referencing Section 77(7) of the Electoral Act, which provides that a political party that fails to comply with the Act’s requirements for nominating candidates shall not be allowed to nominate a candidate for the affected position.
The lawyer explained that the Electoral Act does not allow a petitioner to challenge a candidate’s nomination and automatically replace that candidate if the court finds the nomination violated the law. Rather, the party risks losing the opportunity to field a candidate for the affected position.
There have been allegations that Mr Omo-Agege did not participate in the NDC’s primary election before the party nominated him as its candidate. If established, this action would violate the Electoral Act.
Mr Eni-Otu, however, argued that, under the Electoral Act, only aspirants who participated in a party’s primary election can challenge the nomination of the candidate who emerged from the process.
He also predicted that Mr Omo-Agege could pursue the matter to the Supreme Court, noting that it is a pre-election dispute.
The lawyer also highlighted instances in which political parties allegedly deploy internal mechanisms to prevent aspirants from participating in primary elections.
He urged the National Assembly to review and amend the Electoral Act to prevent political parties from deliberately denying aspirants the opportunity to participate in primary elections.
“Most political parties have lots of underhanded acts which are geared towards depriving aspirants of the right to participate in proper primaries and, by extension, the right to challenge the outcome of a primary where such primaries were not conducted in line with the law.
“Going forward, the National Assembly should look into that and find a way to prevent political parties from engaging in acts intended to deprive aspirants of their right to fair hearing and their right to participate freely in a free and proper primary election within the political space,” he said.
